#4017. "Creation without a creator": Pathologic 3's devs have refused to patch an invisible apple tree, and for a blissful moment, I thought they were lying to poison Google's AI

"Maybe this apple tree is trying to tell us something."

Magnificent, depressing plague colony fable Pathologic 3 has received a sizeable game update that adds some new difficulty modes, a photo feature, and some new, worryingly folkloric methods of defeating a murky embodiment of disease. Developers Ice Pick Lodge have also staunchly refused to remove an invisible apple tree, describing this apparently "famous" bug as a hallmark of a game whose "symbolic nature has almost overtaken its function as a product". This appears to be the last major update for Pathologic 3, so that invisible apple tree is staying in the game forever.

I confess, when I first read the Steam blog in question, I doubted. The thing about invisible apple trees is that they are quite easy to confuse with apple trees that are simply not there. Pathologic in general is a house of lies: as Quintin Smith (RPS in peace) put it in his legendary Butchering Pathologic trilogy, "absolutely everybody has an angle, everyone's bending the truth and trying to twist you round their fingers." Pathologic 3 especially is a purgatorial time travel story that must be continually rewritten, a crock of festering rumours enclosed by an enormous, phantom theatre. As such, I read Ice-Pick's typically professorial account of the "invisible apple tree" with intense suspicion.

"Roger Ebert, the famous film critic, once argued that video games could never be art," the devs write on Steam. "It's curious, then, that urinals and bottle racks achieved that status with hardly any struggle, thanks to Marcel Duchamp. So Myst, StarCraft, or Pathologic can't be art, but a urinal can? The distinction, perhaps, lies in function. A urinal placed in a museum stops being plumbing and becomes a symbol. A video game, on the other hand, remains a functional object. We still have to use it.

"But enough about urinals," they go on. "Let's turn to another famous work: Joseph Kosuth's One and Three Chairs. In this work, a chair is no longer simply something to sit on. Whether it's comfortable hardly matters: as a work of art, it still functions. A video game can also become a symbolic chair. But you still have to sit on it. There's a running joke that Pathologic is a great game that nobody actually plays. Somehow, it really has become something like Kosuth's symbolic chair, one nobody is obliged to sit on. Which raises a question: should we even fix Pathologic if its symbolic nature has almost overtaken its function as a product?

"Take visual bugs, for instance. Are they broken chairs you can't sit on, or artistic decisions?" Ice-Pick continue. "Consider our famous invisible apple tree. Oh, apple tree! Why are you here? What are we supposed to do with you? This is probably the most famous bug in Pathologic 3. We've received more complaints about it than almost anything else. We have to admit there were moments when we genuinely hated that tree. Are we going to fix it in this update? Perhaps not.

"After all, it's a creation of the machine," they conclude. "Somehow, the game's code produced this impossible object. And over time, our annoyance at it has begun to turn into a strange affection. Sometimes an artistic act lies not in creating something, but in the artist's decision about it. Maybe this apple tree is trying to tell us something. So the tree stays."

Aside from making me pine for a world in which, say, EA add a "hypernormalisation" slider to The Sims, or Ubisoft redefine Assassin's Creed parkour as a Situationist dérive (yes, I too have read books), the blog post filled me with confusion. I couldn't remember any invisible apple trees in Pathologic 3. I also couldn't find any English language mention of Pathologic 3's avowedly "famous" ethereal vegetation on Google or the Steam forums, save for in stories covering the game's latest update.

My weakness for talk of symbolism notwithstanding, I began to worry that Ice-Pick might be winding us up. And by "us", I specifically mean pathetic videogame reporters, hunting for a cool bug anecdote to wrap a headline around. Pathetic videogame reporters who are subject to the wiles of Google Search, which has recently become an AI-driven abomination that subsumes and rewords all knowledge while starving actual information sources of traffic.

There have been efforts to screw with Google's AI summaries, planting nonsense on Reddit and elsewhere in the hope of skewing or outright sabotaging the chatbot's datasets. Perhaps Pathologic 3's "invisible apple tree" was one such poison apple, I mused to myself, offered to Gemini in the manner of a cackling forest hag thrusting suspiciously plump and juicy fruit at cherubic village children. Associations foamed in my brain: Ice-Pick Lodge are based in Kazakhstan... where apples first grew in the wild. Breathless, I contacted Ice-Pick Lodge for a clarification, and – bah, it turns out there is an invisible apple tree in Pathologic 3, after all.

"The slightly longer story goes like this," producer Alexander Souslov told me over DM. "At some point (nobody remembers exactly when), one of our tree assets - an apple tree, to be precise - started rendering incorrectly and became invisible. The leaves were still there, but the trunk was gone. We tried to fix it, but ran into the classic game developer's dilemma: is this really important enough to spend resources on, rather than, say, making another cutscene or putting together another quest?"

Souslov says the apple tree drove him "absolutely nuts". (I feel like he could have rolled with some line about "one bad apple spoiling the barrel", but hey, I'm not one of those stuffed shirts over at Edge Magazine - I don't mind interviewees mixing their arboreal metaphors.) Eventually, however, he made peace with the exasperatingly trunkless tree. "I started thinking: wait a minute, this thing basically came into existence all by itself. Do I really have to fix it?

"And that's when I remembered Marcel Duchamp and his ideas, and suddenly I began to feel that we'd accidentally created something beautiful," Souslov went on. "Invisible trees next to the Cathedral, where time flows in different directions. There's a strange kind of beauty in that, in the very act of creation without a creator.

"So I made an executive artistic decision: we're keeping the tree, and we're officially declaring it part of the world. So no pranks involved! Just a happy accident elevated to the status of artistic intent."

With Souslov's guidance, I fired up an old Pathologic 3 save and tracked down the invisible apple tree in-game, right next to the aforesaid Cathedral. Please find a picture of the thing's spectral foliage below – poetically captured by moonlight at the dead of 1am, through a fog of in-game Apathy. I also belatedly checked Reddit, and yep, there's a paper trail, though Souslov added that the bug is inconsistent: "their whimsical behavior makes it even better as an artistic expression - the apple tree may decide it won't meet with you today."

I remain compelled by the idea of developers telling dirty great porkies in their patchnotes, if only to excite and upset games journalists who really don't have this much time to spare. Mojang used to do that thing with Herobrine, remember?

Given the escalating chatbotification of everything, I think we are entering an exhilarating new age of lying on the internet, in which deceit and doublespeak have become weapons of resistance against the algorithm. But I also just think videogames and their creators are often more fun when they are two-faced, providing there's some fundamental benevolence involved. Videogames are all about sleight of hand, and devs should take more pleasure in that. Thank you to Pathologic 3 for planting this seed.

Stardew Valley creator Eric "ConcernedApe" Barone has been hard at work on the 1.7 update for some time now, teasing fans about what to expect – and it sounds like it'll bring much more than just two new marriage candidates to the table.

We already know we'll be able to romance Clint and Sandy come 1.7, and that we'll get a new farm type with the update. It sounds big enough as is, considering just those elements and the other social features ConcernedApe has teased – but it's not just big, y'all. According to the mastermind developer, it might just be the biggest that Stardew Valley has ever seen… even bigger than 1.5 and 1.6, which boasted added regions, festivals, and more.

He reveals as much during a recent Stardew Valley Symphony of Seasons concert at the Red Rocks Amphitheatre in Colorado, as posted over on Reddit by an attending fan. After recalling how incredible his farming sim's growth has been, he mentions the patch that's on everyone's mind. "We're working on the 1.7 update, which is looking to be the largest Stardew Valley update ever," he says. "It's jam-packed."

ConcernedApe doesn't stop there, either. In his own words, "Clint and Sandy are just the tip of the iceberg – there's so much more in the update." He even drops a release hint: "You guys are in for a real treat, and it'll probably come out sometime next year." Next year is just a couple of months away at this point, which means we could get the new Stardew Valley update a whole lot sooner than expected (should the stars align, of course).

There are a good few months in 2027, though – you know, a whole 12 of 'em – so there's no telling just yet whether or not we'll get 1.7 toward the start of the year or the tail end. I'll be keeping my fingers crossed for the former, but ConcernedApe's a busy guy. He's got Haunted Chocolatier to grapple with, too, which he previously admitted is "taking a long time" to get right – but getting things right is his priority.

Microsoft says this console was created by John Nolan Studio, which has worked on loads of famous projects including Jurassic World Dominion and the upcoming Harry Potter series for HBO Max.

There's only one of them as mentioned, and the way to enter the sweepstakes is by following these instructions:

It's worth noting here that the giveaway is only for residents of the United States, and entries close in exactly a week. The chances of securing it are extremely slim, of course, but you've got to be in it to win it!

#4014. Control Resonant Is Remedy's Fastest Selling Game Ever, Led to a Massive Boost in Revenue

Publisher and developer Remedy Entertainment recently released its latest game, Control Resonant, and it's been a big success so far.

In fact, it's the fastest-selling game ever for the company, reaching 1 million copies sold just three weeks after launch.

As a result, Remedy has enjoyed a very strong third quarter, as outlined in its latest financial report.

Essentially, the launch of Control Resonant meant the company's Q3 — from July to September 2026 — saw a big year-on-year jump in revenue, up 226 per cent.

Operating profit also dramatically increased; Remedy reports €0.6 million, a significant boost from the €16.4 million loss it reported for the same period last year.

The company says the US is the game's largest market on both PC and consoles, accounting for "nearly half" of all sales.

It also says that nearly half of all players are "new to Control", suggesting the audience for the series has expanded substantially with the arrival of Resonant.

By all accounts, it seems the game has done very well for Remedy, then. We really liked the game in our review, as did many other critics, and it sounds like it's doing well commercially too.

#4013. Ghost of Yotei studio Sucker Punch reportedly lays off 26 developers "after carefully observing the challenges in the market"

The PlayStation-owned developer is making cuts.

Layoffs have reportedly hit Sucker Punch, the PlayStation-owned studio behind the Sly Cooper series, Infamous and last year's Ghost of Yotei.

Aftermath reports that 26 workers have been affected by the cuts, citing a former employee. According to an email sent to staff and seen by Aftermath, studio leadership blamed layoffs on the shaky state of the industry and "the needs" of the developer's next, unannounced game.

"After carefully observing the challenges in the market and reviewing the team needs for our next project, we've decided to make some staffing reductions. Several positions across Sucker Punch will be eliminated as a result," studio higher ups wrote.

"We know this is a lot to take in, and we want to assure you that we did not make this decision lightly. We have given this a lot of attention and worked to support our affected colleagues during this transition as well as we can… There's no getting around that this is a hard day. Next week we will go into more details about the future."

Sucker Punch's last game, the gorgeous open-world sequel Ghost of Yotei, was seemingly a big hit for PlayStation. Ghost of Yotei sold 3.3m copies about a month after launch, outperforming other PS5 favourites such as Astro Bot in the same time period.

While Sony hasn't published updated financial figures since then, the console maker did say Ghost of Yotei "exceeded the sales of the previous title in the same period of time" when reporting its financials for the quarter ending on the 31st of December. Ghost of Tsushima sold upwards of 13m copies across consoles and PC, though Sony is seemingly done bringing its signature single-player games to PC. As ever in the games industry, even success can't protect talented developers from layoffs.

This summer's Ghost of Yotei: Complete Edition re-release came with an interesting roguelike mode, additional cosmetics, a story-focused bonus episode called Echoes of Sekigahara and much more.

#4012. "We basically rewrote the entire State of Decay game": Undead Labs spent years trying to make State of Decay 3 into a full-blown zombie apocalypse MMO

State of Decay 3 was announced with a snazzy cinematic trailer all the way back in 2020. The open-world zombie game was due to move to colder climes, where you would face undead deer and survive the frigid elements. We've since learned that the teaser bore very little resemblance to what was actually being worked on, and was pushed out the door to plump up a Microsoft showcase.

However, what the teaser also didn't reveal was that Undead Labs' ideas for the game were much larger in scope than the two survival games that came before. For several years they were trying to make State of Decay 3 into an MMO that captured the scale of a global zombie apocalypse.

In an interview with GamesIndustry.biz detailing the recent move to independence after Xbox cut the studio loose, Undead Labs CEO Philip Holt explains that the team's founder, Jeff Strain, planned to expand the series from its co-op roots into a full MMO. While Strain left the studio in 2019, his ideas remained with the small team working on the prototypes for State of Decay 3. "He always had a vision of making an MMO and the ultimate global scale of a zombie apocalypse," Holt says. "And so there was just a different set of creative objectives the team was trying to pursue at that time."

After State of Decay 3 was announced in 2020, a small team worked on developing the technology to support an MMO, while the rest of the studio continued supporting State of Decay 2. However, towards the end of 2022, Holt and the team decided to go back to a game that better resembled the scale of the first two games. "There was a pretty significant pivot creatively on State of Decay 3's development," Holt tells GI. "So I would say the game that's present today has really been built probably since '23, maybe late '22." Later in the interview saying "One of the things I learned is just how much respect I have for teams that make successful MMOs, because I've seen them swallow people whole."

It wasn't a flippant change, as it meant throwing out much of what had already been made. "We basically rewrote the entire State of Decay game, and we will not do that again," Holt says. "We have the benefit now of this pretty significant investment in software that we got to figure out how to make the most of. We hope that State of Decay 3 has a long and successful life and becomes a live and evolving game. But yeah, I think it's highly unlikely that we spend as much time on the next game as we did on State of Decay 3."

Though, it did mean that when Xbox cut ties with Undead Labs they had a project near enough to release that they've been able to find a publisher willing to fund State of Decay 3's final months of development. Still, even with that support, Undead Labs still had to lay off "a significant number" of staff.

I've a real soft spot for the state of Decay games, though I've never played them in multiplayer. For me, they were always an apocalypse I could mooch around in solo, gradually expanding my survivors' camp and making a dent in the zombie hordes that roamed across the environment. An MMO take on the same world wouldn't have appealed to my misanthropic sensibilities, but I'm interested to learn how the tech that was produced has been rolled into the current version of State of Decay 3.

Still, one day, I want to face down a zombie deer. Granted, I'll immediately run and hide, but it'd be nice to see one.

Remake had a bigger job – setting up what would follow

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Final Fantasy 7 Remake trilogy lead Naoki Hamaguchi may be working towards what's shaping up to be the biggest and boldest installment yet, the grand finale of Revelation, but it turns out that, of the three, the first game was the hardest to make.

In an interview with French content creator mistermv, translated by Genki on Twitter (and verified by GamesRadar+), Hamaguchi is asked what the biggest development challenge of the trilogy has been, and he immediately points back to where it all began.

For a start, the development team was much smaller in the beginning. At first, Hamaguchi notes, the team was only comprised of 30 people – a number obviously eclipsed by the final credits on the game.

But more than that, Remake also had the challenge of setting up what would follow it. The start of the project meant deciding on the entire visual look and graphical quality for the Remake trilogy, for example, all while working to the pressure of pleasing the many massive FF7 fans, with the worry of the devs' efforts being insufficient in meeting players' lofty expectations.

On the other hand, Rebirth and Revelation were able to follow in the footsteps of the foundation built by Remake – while they may have been larger and more ambitious, as Hamaguchi puts it, they had a base to go on, and the team working on them had grown and evolved, too.

Hamaguchi and other FF leads have previously spoken about how creating the Final Fantasy 7 remake in the trilogy format has allowed the devs to take on feedback between installments, too, hopefully making each experience better than the last for players. For example, Hamaguchi is aware that many players felt that Rebirth had an overwhelming amount of content, and while Revelation "probably" has even more, the devs have made some key differences in signposting what side-content will earn you what rewards, and ultimately making it easier for players to decide what they care about pursuing.

Final Fantasy 7 Revelation has a hard mode you can select from the start, Naoki Hamaguchi says, but it "won't function in the exact same way as it did in Remake and Rebirth."

#4009. Amid sweeping layoffs at Xbox and massive AI investments, Microsoft introduces a "Voluntary Exit Offer" to 60,000 workers

Xbox isn't the only Microsoft division looking to massively reduce worker headcounts. In fact, Microsoft has just announced a "Voluntary Exit Offer" that will essentially pay staff to move in front of any potential layoffs and voluntarily leave their jobs.

Microsoft CPO Amy Coleman announced the plan earlier today. "This offer gives eligible employees who may be considering a future outside the company a new choice to make that transition now with support. It also gives participating organizations another way to adapt their workforce to changing needs," Colemon wrote in a memo sent to staff.

The voluntary buyout is only available to Microsoft employees "at level 70 and below" in Canada, India, the United Kingdom and the United States. Some corners of the company have opted out of the offer - it's currently unclear if Xbox or any of the studios under its umbrella are participating in the initiative.

"This is a time-limited, voluntary program that gives those who are eligible the opportunity to leave Microsoft with financial support and career planning resources. Some organizations are providing the Voluntary Exit Offer, and some are not. Participation varies based on each business’s priorities, customer commitments and workforce needs," Coleman added.

A Microsoft spokesperson told Business Insider that the offer will be available to about 60,000 employees, roughly 25 percent of the company's total workforce - a staggering figure. According to the outlet, Microsoft's voluntary exit offer has similar terms to the company's severance packages, and eligible workers need to decide if they'll lay themselves off by early December.

Xbox embarked on a huge "reset" earlier this year, which involved a planned 3,200 jobs cuts and a massive internal restructure for many of its first-party studios. Double Fine, Compulsion Games and Undead Labs have all gone independent since then, while the fates of Arkane Lyon and Ninja Theory are still shaky. As CNBC noted, the voluntary buyout was announced as Microsoft tries to balance its sky-high spending in generative AI.

#4007. Helldivers 2's Ever-Changing Universe Evolves Again with New Venomous Terminids

One of the best things about Helldivers 2 is its shifting warfront across the shared online galaxy.

Developer Arrowhead has been able to constantly update the game with new missions, narrative beats, and features in this sort of "live" scenario, reacting to how players are doing and shifting the balance to keep things constantly engaging.

It's a really cool aspect of the game, and the latest addition is a dangerous new strain of Terminids.

As detailed on the PS Blog, these new bugs are venomous, and are burrowing beneath the surface, creating highly toxic new cave systems on various planets.

These Terminids move faster, but are more fragile than the regular species. The advice is to use powerful but less precise weaponry, such as shotguns, flamethrowers, and grenades to deal with them quickly.

If you let them attack you, you'll be poisoned. Light poison steadily chips away at your health, while heavy poison stacks over time.

Again, I think it's pretty cool how the game is able to change things up like this. I reckon it's a big reason why Helldivers 2 took off and continues to be popular.

Anyway, will you be blasting these new Terminids in Helldivers 2? Tell us in the comments section below.

#4006. Hot Wax sets fire to the Tetris playbook with slow-burn puzzle mechanics and a dollop of eldritch menace

Over the past couple of weeks, I've been conscious of an eerie background humming and hissing. For a while I thought it was just tinnitus, brought on by one too many listens of Control's Ashtray Maze OST, but then I realised that it was actually RPS regular quasiotter whispering in my ear about Hot Wax, which launches on Steam this week after a spell of Itch.io exclusivity.

It's the new arcade puzzler from PUNKCAKE Délicieux, otherwise known for inflicting shotguns on chess and forcing the alphabet to wear trousers in the name of archaeology, somehow. Hot Wax is actually quite straightforward by PUNKCAKE standards. It's Tetris, but all the blocks are candles, and rather than filling a line on the grid to clear blocks, you have to plant unpredictably dropped flames on wicks to slowly sizzle the mass away. Relatively straightforward, yes, but fiddly in practice. Did I mention that you're doing all this in a temple, under the eye of a "not unfriendly" eldritch god?

There's still a demo for Hot Wax on Steam, with the full release due in Valve's cathedral of commerce tomorrow. I've had a go at that demo, and it has tickled my brain. You need to line up candles, wick to wick, rather than just filling gaps, as in Tetris. But you still, ideally, need to avoid gaps to slow down the filling of the screen. Once a wick is lit, it'll gradually melt the candle and leap to any other wicks it touches.

Once a candle is lit, you have to avoid smothering it by unscientifically dunking another candle on top of it, while trying to take advantage of how the melting wax alters the layout. I found this enjoyably challenging. And then there are the power-up items, acquired by sacrificing flames to the aforesaid "not unfriendly" god. These include bombs that light a bunch of wicks at once, and acorns that sprout a column-filling sapling. Not sure what they worship in this temple, exactly, other than Tetris.

There will be a bunch of modes in the full release – from basic score attack and endless play, to a mode where you have to melt several, painstakingly arranged candles with just one flame. They're also planning daily seeded challenge runs. As with PUNKCAKE stuff at large, it's a looker, with some lustrous pixel art and lots of nifty little animations. Thank you, quasiotter – this was fun! You can stop going "EEEEEEEE" in my ear now.

#4005. Mass Effect fans ramp up efforts to save BioWare's RPG series with a Times Square billboard and plans for more ads outside The Game Awards

Fans continue to rally around the 'Save Mass Effect' movement, this time with a billboard at Times Square and more initiatives planned throughout the rest of the year.

Last week, publisher EA shut down BioWare and cancelled the next Mass Effect game. In the days since, an increasingly loud community-organised campaign has attempted to make Electronic Arts reverse course and ensure that the beloved sci-fi universe can journey forward in some form.

🚨 WE'RE IN TIMES SQUARE! Together with @kalaelizabeth, we've managed to get a #SaveMassEffect billboard up in Times Square, NYC, all day today! 📍 1560 Broadway, above the Pelé store (Duffy Square) ⏰ 15 seconds every hour at :35 HOLD THE LINE! ❤️ https://t.co/wNP9Ak9Vh8

The We Are Mass Effect community group and content creator Kala Elizabeth are now collaborating on a number of initiatives, including a billboard at New York City's Times Square that points people toward the growing online "SaveMassEffect" hashtag. Text that reads "Kellah Si'yah" is sprawled across the ad - referencing the in-game ship that ferried different races to settle the Andromeda system.

"Apart from the Times Square billboard, we also have several other initiatives in the works. An advertising truck near EA's headquarters in Redwood City and in Edmonton, a mobile billboard for N7 Day, and another one in LA for The Game Awards. All of them will carry a message in support of #SaveMassEffect," one of the group's organisers, Mer Mora, told me via email.

The 'SaveMassEffect' petition gained a huge amount of traction this weekend with 226,000 signatures and counting. The petition urges rights holder EA to commit to "the continued development of Mass Effect" by either funding a new game in the series or by licensing it to an outside studio who can do it justice.

"All of these initiatives will be funded by the community itself! We're putting together a GoFundMe after receiving an overwhelming response from community members eager to contribute financially to make all of these happen," Mora added. "And given the incredible support and generosity we've received, any funds raised beyond our goal will be donated to the Game Workers' Hardship Fund, which supports game developers who have been laid off." The United Videogame Workers union (UVW-CWA) opened the fund earlier this year to support the many laid off video game workers across Canada and the USA.

Marvel fans have noticed that the Avengers: Doomsday artwork reveals a key detail about the X-Men storyline

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Just over a month before the new MCU movie lands in cinemas, new Avengers: Doomsday artwork has found its way online, but a closer look at the X-Men reveals an interesting detail about Ian McKellen's Magneto.

The images were shared on Twitter by French fansite HexFacility, which has been known to share legit Marvel leaks in the past. Although we cannot confirm that the images have come from Marvel Studios, it looks like the artwork has been taken from Hasbro's Marvel Legends Avengers: Doomsday Series, as many of the images line up with the heroes' action-figure counterparts and the packaging.

The new images give us a new look at Captain America, Thor, Doctor Doom, Yelena Belova, Bucky Barnes, Red Guardian, Sue Storm, Reed Richards, the Thing, M'Baku, Shuri, and more.

The artwork also features X-Men Professor X, Magneto, Gambit, Cyclops, Mystique, Nightcrawler, and Beast. However, one Marvel fan on Reddit has noticed an interesting detail about Magneto. If you take a closer look, you can see that most of the mutants are wearing an X belt to signify they are part of Charles' X-Men squad, including Magneto. Check out the images below.

⬣ AVENGERS: Doomsday - Visuels Promo pour le Professeur Xavier, Magneto, et Nightcrawler ! https://t.co/MAlFKJwENYNovember 2, 2026

"I love how everyone has the X mark on their belts, even Magneto. It shows everyone is on the same side, despite Magneto and Mystique being rivals in the past," said the fan. Although we cannot see the front of Mystique's belt, it looks like she too is sporting the X-Men uniform. In the original Fox-era X-Men trilogy, Charles and Erik were often at odds, with Erik, aka Magneto, often waging war on the human race. But Charles was always there with his mutants to make him see sense.

We already knew that the two would be somewhat civil in the new movie. In the Avengers: Doomsday trailer, we see them sitting together, looking pretty terrified as their universe faces destruction from Doctor Doom. Alongside McKellan and the late Patrick Stewart as Professor X, Doomsday welcomes back original X-Men James Marsden as Cyclops, Rebecca Romijn as Mystique, Alan Cumming as Nightcrawler, and Kelsey Grammer as Beast, and adds Deadpool and Wolverine's Channing Tatum as Gambit.

But Magneto doesn't really have a choice either way, as everyone is going to have to work together if they have any chance of stopping Robert Downey Jr.'s Victor Von Doom. As the official synopsis reads, "Doomsday is set to bring beloved heroes from three distinct universes together as they’re set on a deadly collision course and face an existential threat unlike anything they’ve ever encountered."

#4003. Subnautica 2 dev thinks early access teams should worry less about adding features that are "very ugly, incomplete, or prototype"

But acknowledges that "early access" ain't what it was

Subnautica 2 creative director Anthony Gallegos has spoken about what Unknown Worlds have learned over their many years working in Steam early access, exhorting other devs to add new features "as soon as possible" and experiment with them right under the flared nostrils of players. Damn the torpedoes, etcetera.

The original Subnautica is one of the oldest Steam early access success stories, launching in 2014 a month or so after the program went live. Many of the final version's better qualities, including the pivot to horror epitomised by the spectacle of a Reaper grabbing your submarine's face, reflect observation of players and streamers in the wilds.

"Subnautica often launched features when they were very ugly, incomplete, or prototype," Gallegos commented, as part of a group chat about early access with GamesIndustry.biz. "This gave fans a real sense of getting to see game development in progress, in a way few other studios would try, especially for a franchise as big as this."

Unknown Worlds have "cultivated a very empathetic audience through radical transparency," Gallegos continued. "We trust the audience to give us a little grace as we figure things out, and they in turn trust us to make it great in the fullness of time."

Naturally, Gallegos thinks it's vital to keep talking to players and taking their feedback on the chin. "Be honest with them and make them understand how crucial they are to the process," he went on. "Preserve your vision, but listen to them and let them help you bring the best out of your game." Early access remains "core" to the "DNA" of Unknown Worlds, as they continue with the creation of Subnautica 2, which is about to get a nourishing injection of robot frogs.

I'm writing this up mostly because I'd like to know where you all stand as regards the "very ugly, incomplete, or prototype" - which, now that I think about it, sounds like the film Sergio Leone might have made, if he'd gotten into industry documentaries rather than spaghetti westerns. My view on early access is basically that it has become the same things as live service. I'm not sure there's a meaningful division any more between labelling a game "unfinished" and the expectation that devs will keep adding stuff to any release.

Within that, though, there's a lot of diversity, as Gallegos acknowledges in the GI piece. "Early access could mean a game like ours doing long-term open development, or it could be a game three months from a 1.0 release that's effectively doing a paid beta soft launch and using the Early Access term as a way to soften player expectations," he observed.

Not everybody has been as fortunate as Unknown Worlds in persuading players to give them the benefit of the doubt. In a crowded market (GI say that 2,924 early access games have launched on Steam this year so far, citing SteamDB), newer teams may suffer from being compared to older operators like Unknown Worlds, who got involved when early access was still fresh and exotic.

Elsewhere in the GI article, Denis Dyack, CEO of Deadhaus Sonata developer Apocalypse Studios, argues that expectations are unavoidably set by the early access devs with the largest budgets, citing Subnautica 2 as an example.

Back to you, the atrocious buyer of unfinshed games: what do you expect from an early access release? What degree of wobble will you overlook? What are you happy for devs to leave out till the final version? How important is communication, really? Does it just depend totally on the game? Here is some topical music to think along to.

#4002. Assassin's Creed Black Flag Resynced's final major update adds long-awaited New Game Plus, new Nightmare difficulty and much more

After a period of quiet and a few small updates, Ubisoft has unveiled a massive update coming today to Assassin's Creed Black Flag Resynced. This is the game's last major patch and it includes some long-requested features.

Update 1.0.8 goes live on PC, PS5 and Xbox Series X/S today (27th October) at 7am PT, 10am ET, 2pm UK. It's a relatively small download on all platforms - between 2 and 4.5GB - except Xbox, where it's a whopping 15.5GB.

The new update's biggest addition is New Game Plus mode, which Ubisoft started working on in July after releasing Resynced. Much of what's earned and unlocked in your current playthrough carries over to NG+, but not everything does. Here's what carries over:

While cash and trade goods do carry over, quest-related items do not. Forts also need to be re-taken, as NG+ resets the map's fog of war.

The NG+ mode has a new exclusive currency - Escudos - earned by completing challenges and looting previously unlocked chests. The currency can be spent on NG+ exclusive outfits and items, and you'll be able to exchange Reales for Escudos at the General Store, too.

Naturally, the game difficulty increases with each NG+ run. Elite soldiers, for instance, will appear more often, and max rank ships will be a more common sight across the water. You can enter NG+ up to five times, with each further runthrough increasing the challenge.

Patch 1.0.8 also introduces Nightmare Mode, a new brutal difficulty setting. Ubisoft said enemy reaction times and the damage they deal are ramped up. Parry timings are tighter, and ranged enemies will target you more often.

What may be the biggest change, however, is the removal of the one-shot kill safety. In other words, the game won't prevent you from receiving instant deaths, such as in cases where you take high burst damage from bullets and explosives. In those cases, you're going to die, even if you have HP left. The goal was to create a harsh experience "where every duel can be your last".

Elsewhere in the patch, there are new community chests hidden around the game's world for players to uncover. There's a set of new cosmetics, new takedown animations, and, of course, a litany of bug fixes. The full change log is on the official Assassin's Creed website. It's worth reading if you're looking to attempt a playthrough on Nightmare to see what it changes.

Though that may be Assassin's Creed Black Flag Resynced's last big update, the game is seemingly on its way to Switch 2, and that version should include all previously-released additions, as we've come to expect.

#4001. The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel Is Still 'At Least Two Years Away' as Disappointment Follows New Trailer

If you thought that the re-reveal for The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel was signalling some kind of blowout in the relatively near future, then I've got bad news for you.

Reiterating that the finished game is still a long way off, the ever-informative Jason Schreier made things clear on social media, posting: "Sorry to say [The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel] is still more than 2 years away!"

I think a lot of people forget that The Elder Scrolls VI was only announced in 2018 (along with Starfield) to soften the blow of Fallout 76 — "Don't worry, even though we're making a multiplayer game we've got single-player stuff coming too!" Sorry to say this game is still more than 2 years away!

As alluded, this lines up with all of the reports we've had on the project over the last year or so. That doesn't make the realisation any less disappointing, though.

You may recall that the game's development "passed a big milestone" back in February, when Bethesda boss Todd Howard enthusiastically claimed that the project was "coming together".

However, Howard also stressed that Sentinel was "going to be a while yet".

Flash forward to July and Schreier was busy answering questions about the RPG's progress. Despite being in a playable state, the journalist stated that it remained "two to three years away at least".

He's obviously backed this information up with his latest take on the matter.

Then, just a day later, news broke of significant layoffs at Xbox, and subsequently, Bethesda. Over 50 people who were working on Sentinel were reportedly cut loose, sparking concerns over the project's already troubled timeline.

It was said that studio morale was at "rock bottom".

Whether things have changed all these months later we don't know, but this has clearly been a pivotal year for Bethesda and the project.

There's a strong suggestion that Sentinel needs to be a hit, for the studio's sake — and so Todd and the team will be desperate to get it right.

As a quick reminder, The Elder Scrolls 6 was first announced in 2018 (!) with a very short teaser trailer. But as Schreier notes, it was mostly shown to placate the single player masses after the unveiling of the multiplayer-focused Fallout 76.

It'll be the 15th anniversary of Skyrim next week, which is insane to think about, and really puts this whole timeline into perspective.

When do you expect The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel to release? Keep your expectations in check in the comments section below.

The Wardogs team is planning to take a long break to celebrate the success of its early access release, and CEO Joe Brammer knows that it'll probably be fine because players will have plenty to occupy them – in the form of GTA 6.

Speaking to Edge Magazine, Brammer explains that the team has worked hard to earn the right to play hard. "Everyone has done something that's not in their job description. Everyone wears multiple hats, because they can see the path to success with the product."

With the early access launch of Wardogs in the rear-view, the entirety of developer Bulkhead Studios will be taking an extended break, with leave stretching throughout the entire month of December. It's a bold strategy, but one that Brammer is quick to double-down on.

"We're going to make sure players know they can fuck off in December," he says, suggesting the team does have some idea of the backlog of bug reports and balance complaints that could be waiting for them come January. The hope, clearly, is that those players will be too distracted by something else to be blasting the Bulkhead forums: "Go play GTA 6, we need to detox," Brammer says.

With most games wondering how they'll hope to hold onto their audiences once Rockstar drops its nuke – and Fortnite offering near-unlimited freebies to certain lucky players – it's almost refreshing to see a team unapologetically accepting that its fans will have something else on their minds, and hoping that they'll come back once they're finished with Leonida.

#3999. "We are more concerned about the risks of moving too slowly": Epic get more specific about genAI use in Unreal Engine and Fortnite development

Epic Games are, dunno if you've heard, on a bit of a genAI kick at the moment. It's been tough to notice unless you listen very hard. Tim Sweeney's lips have been sealed and no reports have spewed forth.

Sark aside, to this point Epic have had far more provocative soundbites and weird marketing lingo to offer than specific detail about how they're using genAI in different parts of their business.

Responding to questioning from This Week in Videogames, Epic's executive vice president of development Marcus Wassmer's run through some of the exact tools and uses that make up the company's current deployment of the tech.

"There are a number of tools in use but probably the most obvious ones are Claude Code and Codex with their associated AI models," he said "They’re helping across a broad spectrum of development, with some particularly big recent wins being almost the complete elimination of non-deterministic cooking bugs which we’ve been fighting for a decade and an acceleration of work related to compressing shaders which both significantly reduce patch sizes. [Other wins include] a rewrite of a significant portion of the D3D12 rendering layer (which I estimated as needing three to six weeks of work for a single engineer, but the work was actually completed in about one week with a nice win on CPU time and fewer bugs), lots of help in keeping our internal test suites healthy as well as expanding those test suites for more coverage."

Wassmer went on to add that Fortnite's seen the additions of "automatic monitoring of PC stability", "automatic root cause analysis and automatic fix generation", which he claims have sped up the rectifying of long-running issues. He also noted that, engine-wise, Epic have been able to attempt "some larger architectural refactors with AI" than they previously could due to the amount of file changes required.

The dev went on to confirm that the Epic Store launcher preview released the other week isn't the only bit of vibe-coding the company have been up to, with the practice also being used in Unreal Engine development. "Yes, we are vibe-coding things," he said. "That means our engineers are no longer writing the bulk of the code, but they are still guiding the tools to get the architectural result we want. We’re not ‘one-shotting’ the engine; we’re iterating with AI to ship features developers want and keep the engine within the memory, performance, and scalability envelopes."

Wassmer also managed to fit in some justification as to why Epic see no other way forward then shoving a bunch of genAI into their development, largely parroting the typical talking point of 'everyone's going to be doing it soon and we can't possibly be seen to miss out on that gold rush for short-term speediness, baby'. "We are more concerned about the risks of moving too slowly than we are about AI skepticism," is one of the lines he actually said.

To be fair, at least Wassmer and Epic aren't hiding the fact they're embracing this stuff, as much as Timmy Sweens hates the concept of devs having to disclose their genAI use to prospective customers or users. Sometimes the desire of AI bros to shout about their use from the rooftops out of sheer marketing zeal has its positives, eh?

#3998. Composer shares 20 minutes of music created for Mass Effect 5 following tragic closure of BioWare

Austin Wintory has shared twenty minutes of music they pitched to BioWare and EA in hopes of joining the Mass Effect 5 development team, following the tragic closure of BioWare last week.

The composer, known for his work on Journey and Sword of the Sea, uploaded the music to his personal YouTube channel. It was made without knowledge of the narrative direction of the new Mass Effect game, but was presented as a surprise to the companies in 2025 as part of years of conversation. Wintory writes in the video that it was a "direct homage" to Mass Effect 1 composers Jack Wall and Sam Hulick, leaning into analog synths and "a more complex integration of the orchestra", a hybrid approach Wintory compares to The Matrix movies scores.

This collection of music includes a track called The Legacy of Shepard, which includes "deliberate winks" to the original Mass Effect theme. The second track - Sailing the Relays - features the blend of synth and orchestra mentioned earlier quite heavily. All in all, there are eight tracks included in total, with the eighth being a remix of that first Legacy of Shepard composition.

The video's description contains a sombre message on BioWare's closure, as well as gratitude towards the music departments involved in the conversations Wintory took part it: "Receiving the news alongside everyone else that EA had decided to not only cancel the project but shutdown BioWare entirely was a deeply felt loss. It's been hard to see dear friends lose their jobs, and this beloved franchise seemingly vanish forever.

"Thank you nonetheless to everyone at BioWare and EA's music department for gifting me the chance to dream in your sandbox. It was a privilege to do even that much."

Wintory is not alone in their sadness. EA's closure of BioWare, which included the firing of 50 employees and a further 350 across other EA-owned studios, many across the industry came forward to decry the decision. The decision may even have political ramifications, as one Canadian party leader has expressed a desire to allow BioWare employees to buy back the studio with federal support. This all happened shortly after EA's $55bn private acquisition from Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner and Saudi Arabia's Savvy Games Group.

#3997. Try One of 2026's Best PS5 Games on PS Plus Premium Now

The new James Bond simulator from IO Interactive is available to play for 60 minutes on the top tier of the membership service, which begins from the start of the campaign. That one hour of play should see you through the entire prologue mission, Against the Odds, and then you should have enough time left to sample the training mission, The Needle's Eye.

If you like what you play, then your progress will carry over into a full PS5 game purchase. From tomorrow, the Deluxe Edition of 007 First Light will go on sale in the PS Store Black Friday promotion, so you'll be able to pick it up cheaper than full price.

The social media post confirming the Game Trial states it's open to "all PlayStation Plus members", but this isn't actually true. Game Trials are only found on the PS Plus Premium tier.

007 First Light is one of our favourites from 2026, with our PS5 review concluding: "The characterisation of this young Bond and his associates is really strong, and the globetrotting story lets you explore some great locations. It really shines in its sandbox missions, but it weaves these together with its more linear moments in a seamless, cinematic way."

Godzilla Minus Zero is about to make a lot of noise

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Godzilla Minus Zero is so loud that one viewer received repeated "loud environment" warnings from their smartwatch throughout a screening of the super-sized sequel.

Posting on X, content creator @imPatrickT shared an image of the 90 decibel warning, along with a simple statement: "Godzilla Minus Zero is the loudest movie I’ve ever heard in my entire life. This will be a reference title for testing theater setups. Unbelievable film, and the definition of FILMED FOR IMAX."

For reference, 90dB is roughly the volume experienced when standing next to a lawnmower, or a subway train, so that's pretty damn loud. Hearing protection is recommended for sustained exposure to sounds over 80dB. Minus Zero is 'only' 135 minutes long, but you might still want to pack earplugs anyway if you have sensitive ears.

It's been a noteworthy year for loud movies, as many questioned if Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey was too loud. This seemed to be a particular concern in IMAX screenings, where volume levels are set by the filmmaker. The Cyclops' scream and the Poseidon storm were the main culprits, with some reporting that the Cyclops' scream hit as high as 120dB in their screenings.

Of course, it makes sense for Godzilla Minus Zero to turn up the noise, as the sequel will see Big G square off against King Ghidorah, though don't expect it to turn into a "giant pro wrestling match" between two kaiju, according to director Takashi Yamazaki. The movie has already proven a big hit with critics, and in our own Godzilla Minus Zero review, we awarded it 4.5*, calling it "easily one of the best films of the year."

As for what's next, the official trailer promised "everything ends here" and "there will not be a third fight," but Yamazaki recently told SFX that he would "probably say yes" if Toho offered him a third film.

Godzilla Minus Zero releases on November 6. For more, check out our guide to all the most exciting upcoming movies for everything else worth seeing this year (and beyond).

I'm the Managing Editor, Entertainment here at GamesRadar+, overseeing the site's film and TV coverage. In a previous life as a print dinosaur, I was the Deputy Editor of Total Film magazine, and the news editor at SFX magazine. Fun fact: two of my favourite films released on the same day - Blade Runner and The Thing.

#3995. Company of Heroes 3's Operation Torch DLC ships off to North Africa in November, for new missions based around the Allied landings

Atten-shun! Company Of Heroes 3's got new single-player missions inbound via a DLC set during the Allies' 1942 invasion of North Africa. You'll take charge of American forces through a campaign steeped in second world war history that's designed to test your tactical nous and ability to upgrade fighting units to come out on top.It's out on November 25th.

As is made rather obvious by its name, the DLC depicts Operation Torch, which saw the Brits and yanks work together to invade Vichy France-controlled Algeria and Morocco. There's a "dramatic campaign arc that spans the opening invasion, the defeat at Kasserine, and the final assault on Hill 609", no doubt with copious mentions of names like Eisenhower and Patton across its 15 missions.

You'll don the boots of three American soldiers who're either in command or in the thick of the action on the battlefield, with devs Relic noting that their "perspectives reflect the hardships, losses, responsibilities, and lessons learned as they are forged into the fighting force that will liberate Europe".

In between the likes of urban tank battles and stealth ops, you'll pick upgrades earned through completing objectives, ensuring your troops fight in the manner that best suits your preferred tactical slant. For example, I assume you'll be able to go all-in on artillery if all you're after is some big booms that look impressive, but might prove useless if the enemy are safely tucked away in deep cover waving their middle fingers at your boys.

"Company Of Heroes 3 is a rip-roaring return to form and then some for Relic's much loved RTS, and its stirring orchestral score will have you beating your chest and yelling hoo-rah like only the best toy soldier fantasies can," former RPS commander-in-chief Katharine wrote of COH 3 on release in 2023. "If Relic can iron out some of those lingering campaign niggles, this could easily be an all-timer for WWII strategy buffs."

More recently, current boss Julian gave roguelite spin-off Company of Heroes 3: Final Stand a go, coming out with the impression that it's a shakeup which succeded in increasing his appreciation for the series.

#3994. Pokémon Unite closing down for good, but you'll still be able to use it afterwards, sort of

That's it for Pokémon Unite. Tencent's once-popular MOBA is being switched off in March 2027. The Pokémon Company announced the news today, saying: "We regret to inform you that service for Pokémon Unite will end on Tuesday, March 23, 2027, at 00:00 UTC."

By way of thanking people for playing, a "special event" runs from now until service-end, which brings a number of additions to the game. Among them is an intriguing Library feature that lets you continue using the game, to a degree, after its end.

The Library allows you to access the Practice Area of Pokémon Unite to view your earned items - Holowear, cosmetics, Pokémon, and achievements - so your efforts in the game won't entirely disappear. It'll be available starting 12th November. But note that you'll need to use the Library before the 23rd March 2027 switch-off date to get the data Library needs to show your achievements, and because that data's stored locally, you may lose the data if you change device.

"Library data generally cannot be transferred when changing devices," the Pokémon website said. "If the game or library data is deleted or otherwise lost after service ends, it may not be recoverable. Support for the library feature will not be available after service ends."

It seems like a thoughtful way to sunset a game, allowing players a record of their progress and some interactivity, instead of yanking everything away entirely.

Pokémon Unite launched in 2021, first on Switch and then on mobile devices. It's a free-to-play MOBA, essentially, where two teams of five battle it out in an arena with various routes through it and control points to secure and, as Pokémon battle, they earn experience and level up. Pokémon Unite had already been shut down in some European countries because of loot box gambling concerns.

Nine years ago, Matt Filer officially began work on the OpenCAGE mod tools for Alien: Isolation—following two-and-a-half years of work on prototype versions. During that time the tools have been available for anyone to use, which is part of the reason Creative Assembly's legendarily scary horror game has a variety of mods already. (Though the VR mod works differently, since it's actually enabling an unfinished mode that shipped with the game.)

OpenCAGE has finally made it to version 1.0, which can be downloaded on Steam. Filer proudly told us his mod tools have "now reached the point where you're able to implement full custom maps, missions, modes, characters, weapons, animations, sounds, models, textures, and more!"

As a demonstration of what's possible, Filer is making a Halo-themed custom map. "It features custom cinematics, enemies, weapons, all on a brand new map with a custom HUD," he said. "It has reached a point now of being able to make full total conversion mods, which has always been my end goal, so it's cool to finally be here!"

Alien: Isolation just won our scariest videogame poll, and I consider it a well-earned victory. It's one of the few games I've seen frighten even people who aren't normally bothered by horror thanks to how unpredictable and relentless the xenomorph is when pursuing you. And those dead-eyed Worker Joe robots are no slouches either.

Hopefully some creative mods will give us reason to go back to Alien: Isolation, and help tide over the wait for the upcoming Alien: Isolation 2, which is likely to be available some time in 2027.

Beating the Phantom Blade Zero Bai Chilian boss fight isn't easy as this serpentine woman moves erratically and quickly, and can deliver some devastating blows. However, as always with these boss fights, knowledge is power, and so is blocking, parrying, and dodging. Learn Bai Chilian's attack patterns and take in the tactics I've laid out below, and the fight will become much easier to manage – just be aware that there's a second phase that mixes things up a bit!

Bai Chilian, Lady of the Twin Serpents, is a story-critical boss, so you can't progress until you've defeated her. Despite her often-rapid movement, she isn't as difficult to bring down as she seems – if you've already beaten the Phantom Blade Zero Three-Faced Puppet, you should have very few problems! With all of that in mind, here are my tips for beating Bai Chilian in Phantom Blade Zero:

Once you've depleted Bai Chilian's health bar, she'll transform into the Sacrificial Serpent for a second boss fight – thankfully there's a checkpoint! Despite having a radically different moveset since she can now swing around using puppet-like strings, much of the same logic and tactics from phase 1 applies, but here are some additional tips:

Once you've beaten both phases of the Bai Chilian fight, you'll get the Broken Illusory Pipa, a crucial story item that's tied to the Phantom Blade Zero Whence The Weeping quest. You'll also get a very good dual-wield weapon, the White Serpent & Crimson Viper swords, and the Resonance Talisman Accessory, which increases your maximum Sha-Chi – both very useful to have for the journey ahead.

This also marks the end of the Crimson Forest region, as you'll be immediately whisked to the next region. Hopefully you've already completed the Phantom Blade Zero A Healer's Mercy quest and answered the Phantom Blade Zero Nimble Thief questions though!

#3991. Cyberpunk trading sim Probably Stolen is about running a kiosk in a space station full of gangs, megacorps, and secret rogue cyborgs

I will have you know this is an original Malorian Arms 3516

I have so far not been shivved, shanked, brain fried, hazed, wasted, ironed, short-circed, flat-lined or even complained at in Probably Stolen - Cyberpunk Shopkeeper Sim, but I'm sure it's just a matter of time.

In this neuromantic kiosk game from Questing Goose Studio, you're a new store owner aboard a backwater space station. Each day, you roll up the shutter and do business with a procession of shady types, ranging from janitors with unappetising beards to sexy cowled folk with Main Character tattoos. The basics are simple enough, for all the overwhelmingly menu-led presentation: buy what you can afford, according to your instinct for the wider market, sell what you can fit into the customer's budget. But things quickly get complicated.

You've got to watch out for wanted criminals, checking them against mugshots and possibly, reporting them to security. You've got to think about how your transactions shape the opinions of various factions, from revolutionaries through corpo bosses to the mob. You've got to run a magnifying glass over robot hands and cigarette packets, identifying vintage pieces and counterfeits. You've got to head out at night to scrounge stock from the dumps, preferably without getting shivved, shanked, etcetera. You've got to pay the electricity bill. You've got to shoot rogue androids in the CPU.

I've only peeked timidly over the counter of Probably Stolen, which I would cautiously characterise as Papers, Please with a lot more wheeling and dealing, but it feels like there's some decent substance here. I'm particularly intrigued by the idea of diversifying my operations beyond bog-standard checkout work.

"Start as a gunsmith, chemist, water merchant, fence, farmer, or from absolute rock bottom," the Steam page growls. "Every product line has its own profit curve and its own way of ruining you, weapons bring inspections, chemicals bring addiction, water brings liability, contraband brings raids. Some trades need heavy machinery and permits, others just a good hiding spot and a straight face. The better the margins, the worse the consequences when something goes wrong. You’re not choosing a theme for your shop, you’re choosing which kind of trouble you’re willing to monetize."

Oof! I'll use that closing line next time I interview a producer about season passes. Maybe I'll use it next time I have to pick a wallpaper pattern for my flat.

As cyberpunk fictions go, this does seem very comfortable. Your store has a cassette player with a selection of synthy music - I turned it off after 30 seconds, because the tunes were so gratingly generic. Dare I say it, cyberpunk is a "cosy" genre these days, but perhaps I just need to trade up to some classier earworms.

I also don't think much of Probably Stolen's writing, which seems clipped and flavourless, but it's getting the job done, and besides, I'm very early on in my career as a skanky pawnshop operator. I haven't even sold any toilet roll yet, and that feels like the real rite of passage. People who prefer their Netrunner 7-Elevens all 3D and hung with beautiful, beautiful birdcages might prefer the dives you get in No Law, which Julian saw recently.

#3990. Fan favourite map Shipment arrives today in Modern Warfare 4, just four days after launch - a new record for Call of Duty

Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 is getting a small update today that includes the latest iteration of Infinity Ward's iconic Shipment map. The map arrives just four days after Modern Warfare 4's launch last Friday, 23rd October, which is unusually quickly.

Shipment is the original Call of Duty 'small map'. First introduced in Call of Duty 4: Modern Warfare in 2007, the map is designed to offer a breakneck pace of combat no other multiplayer map could. Though there have been Shipment-like small maps over the years - chiefly Treyarch's infamous Nuketown in the Black Ops sub-franchise - nothing could quite replicate Shipment's dizzying rhythm of mayhem.

Shipment's arrival in Modern Warfare 4 was expected, of course; the developer even announced the 27th October release date in a blog post prior to launch. However, joining the roster so close to the game's launch is notable.

Shipment typically arrives two or so weeks post-launch, usually in a game's first live service season. It's been part of Modern Warfare 2019, Modern Warfare 2 (2022), and Modern Warfare 3 (2023). A few other COD titles have versions inspired by it, though not entirely identical, such as COD: WW2's Shipment 1944.

It's long been assumed, perhaps cynically, that Shipment comes just as player numbers start falling off. As one of the series' most popular maps, the thinking is that bringing it back attracts a cohort of the audience who only play that map. It's often used to level up guns, and help get player levels up since the kill count is usually higher than in other, larger maps.

Indeed, Shipment typically releases alongside a dedicated, 24/7 playlist, meaning you don't have to hope for it to show up in the normal map rotation. Infinity Ward didn't say whether we can expect the same playlist this time around, though it is likely.

As with each new iteration, Modern Warfare 4 Shipment features the classic layout but in an entirely new environment inspired by locations from the game. This version has a more urban landscape look that takes after the very first version's muted colours, with Soviet-era concrete buildings in the background. The action takes place in a shipping yard by the harbour, among shipping containers, hence the name.

Incidentally, Modern Warfare 4 is also starting its first season early, with Season One kicking off 6th November, just two weeks after the game's launch, though it is curious Infinity Ward didn't wait until the season's launch to drop the map.

#3989. Ubisoft One of Multiple Companies to Bid for Dishonored Dev Arkane

Ubisoft is one of multiple companies to submit a bid for Dishonored team Arkane Studios, as Microsoft looks to offload the developer in the coming weeks.

That's according to Bloomberg journalist Jason Schreier, who claims that at least two other gaming firms have tried to acquire the developer. No deal has been agreed with Microsoft yet, and Xbox has also weighed up "selling the studio to its management".

Any potential deal is likely to include Arkane being allowed to finish its development of Marvel's Blade, according to the Bloomberg piece, which is set for release in the next year or two. A PS5 version of the game has never been confirmed.

Previously, a cut-off point regarding any potential deal involving Arkane Studios was set for 13th November 2026. That has now been extended by a month, however, to 13th December. Schreier has previously stated he is confident a deal will be struck for Arkane to continue existing under a different owner.

It's hard to overstate Dan's impact over the past 27 years. From shipping Project Gotham Racing on the original XBOX in 2001 to leading the creation of Forza, founding Turn 10 Studios and appearing so many times on our E3 stage, usually making a dramatic entrance with a supercar in tow—and so much more—we owe tremendous thanks and gratitude to Dan. On behalf of both teams, I would like to thank Dan for his leadership, his support, and his partnership. I wish him well for whatever comes next.

The Verge reports that Dan Greenawalt, studio head of Forza Motorsport developer Turn 10, is planning to retire after nearly 27 years, quoting an internal memo from Trevor Williams of Playground Games. "Dan Greenawalt has decided that this is the right time for him to retire from Microsoft," Williams is reported to have said, clarifying that Greenawalt will stay on temporarily as an adviser during a changeover period.

Microsoft announced in September that it plans to merge Turn 10 and Playground, the two Forza studios, into one entity as part of the same restructure that will merge Obsidian into Bethesda and hand Halo over to Activision. Oh, and that restructure will also see another 268 employees being laid off.

Turn 10 had already been turned into a support studio for Playground's Forza Horizon following the 2023 reboot of Forza Motorsport, with former developer Fred Russell saying last year that the Motorsport series died in a prior round of cuts at Microsoft.

The best Rezi 12 builds in MW4 are all about doubling down on the classic strengths of a shotgun: namely the ability to end a foe with a single close-range blast, not bothering too much with accuracy and instead running around cutting through opponents. The Rezi 12 is currently the best shotgun in Modern Warfare 4, and if you make the right sort of build, you can turn it into an absolute killing machine.

For more info on deadly loadouts, check out our list of the best MW4 guns!

Though I've played with a few Rezi builds, this one remains easily the best one in my mind, one based around hipfiring with the Apex Enforcer mod, allowing for explosive slugs and pump-action cycling. This is a build for close-quarters encounters, moving rapidly, and hip-firing. The Heavy Silencer and Heavy Long Barrel are here to ensure maximum impact and effectively guarantee that any shot from the torso up will kill the opponents you encounter.

Meanwhile, the stock (or lack thereof), Assault Grip and Laser are all here to maximize hip fire accuracy and ease of use. This is a build where you fire the moment you see an enemy in close range, and works well as a secondary weapon in an assault loadout, with an AR as your primary.

#3986. GTA 6 has a smell reaction system, which immediately joins Red Dead Redemption 2's dynamically shrinking horse balls on Rockstar's list of immersive symbols of excess

Florida of course being full of smelly smells that smell...smelly

Any reminder of Red Dead Redemption 2's temperature sensitive horse testicles brings a smile to my face. In truth, I can't say I've ever zoomed in close enough to properly take in the spectacle of Arthur Morgan's mount having its nuts dynamically expand and contract based on whether he's riding through snowy mountains or across baking plains, but I do always get a kick out of knowing such a thing's happening as I play. To this point, the horse balls have been the most infamous or meme-worthy example of Rockstar's obsession with going all-in on realistic detail to an arguably unnecessary degree, one that borders on overindulgence which players could conceivably never notice if they weren't expressly told about it.

That philosophy's gone nowhere, so GTA 6 was always going to have a feature that'd become as much of a metaphor for excess as those beloved balls. It may well be the smell reaction system revealed in Edge's long read on the game.

According to this latest rundown of things in GTA 6 and how they were made, Rockstar devs at one point had to make a character react to a not nice smell for a specific bit of "explorable content" stuffed into the game. Cool. One person scrunching their face up to show things are getting stinky in one minigame or mission. Leave it at that.

They reportedly did not leave it at that, later going back to flesh out this one smell reaction into a broader system which other locations to inspire various degrees of face-scrunching by protagonists Lucia and Jason. Cue, in the demo of the game in action which Rockstar gave Edge, Jason walking into a house and starting to act like someone who's just walked into a shower-averse teenager's bedroom during a heatwave despite that not having been set up as part of a deliberately crafted encounter. It's horse ball-esque dynamic systems playing off each other, and voila, a man going eewwwwwwwwwwwww.

Would GTA 6 be any worse off if, as in previous entries, you weren't being shown as expressly which places the crim whose boots you're sharing finds a bit too pongy for their liking? Almost certainly not, but hey, when you've decided your business is taking the detail to levels other games could only dream of having the budget for, getting to the point where you're adding a fiftieth layer of icing to a cake so packed to the gills with different tastes and flourishes that your guests will struggle to appreciate or even notice them all unless you painstakingly point out each one is sort of inevitable.

Another layer of gold wrap on the Bugatti, another brick made of diamonds in a wall projected to be the most lucrative of all time, another farty stench in a room already drowning in foul aromas. It's beautiful in the perverse sort of way that I imagine the Palace of Versailles was to anyone who wandered its gilded halls just prior to the French revolution. To be clear, this isn't any sort of slight on the devs who'll no doubt have worked hard to bring this system and others in GTA 6 to life, a number of whom have a recoginition vote on their unionisation efforts coming up next month.

From a player perspective, one can only hope that by the time GTA 6 hits PC, the RAM crisis has led hardware makers to invest heavily in smellivision tech, so that players around the world can drink in the guffs causing their butt naked on-screen analogue's eyes to water or revel in the stink caused by hitting someone with a bag of dog shit. Forget AI bollocks, this is the future, I scream as I retch into a toilet bowl while some funky tunes from Justice play in the background.

I've played about 50+ hours of the World of Warcraft: Forever beta, and wouldn't you know it, I'm going to be playing a lot more when it comes out November 4.

Earlier this week, Kris Zierhut, principal game designer on World of Warcraft: Forever, said that the game would have a release schedule that's a "little more laid back". Rather than the blisteringly fast eight to 10 week schedule of Season of Discovery, Forever'll aim to release major updates once every four months or so.

This is honestly music to my ears—I've been impressed by retail WoW's blistering pace and its seasonal structure, even if there have been some rocky, bug-filled patches in the past; and it's certainly something I've praised before, especially in contrast to other certain MMOs that have been coming to a standstill.

But I've been playing WoW… well, for a long time, but I've had a consistent sub since Dragonflight, and I've been able to see the arc of Blizzard whipping up its schedule into a proper roadmap. Which did pull the game back from the brink, true, but three expansions in and I'm just sort of exhausted.

There's always some new bar to fill, some new doohickey to collect, some new reputation track to chew on, and it all moves so fast that if I, say, have an off-week to go play another game, I feel pretty lost. While Midnight does major patches at roughly the same release tempo (12.0.0 came out in January, 12.1.0 came out in August) it also has a ton of interim stuff to flood out your schedule every three months, rather than four.

Launch was already crammed with stuff—a raid tier, delves, the new prey system, housing, and so on. Just under three months passed since launch, and wham, suddenly we've got Void Assaults! Ritual Sites! The Omnium Folio! Whatever Abyss Anglers is, I never checked, which is kinda the problem! Just over a month later, and there's a new raid and a new system plugged into Void Assaults (which I'm literally just now finding out about, I completely missed it). Two months later, and it's 12.1.0, which I hadn't even sat down to properly play before Labyrinths became a thing.

The idea of smaller, chiller patches in an overall slower-paced game (here's fellow PCG writer Lincoln Carpenter's treatise on the virtues of hitting a scorpion with a club for 38 seconds) sounds like a nice, soothing bath after an overstimulating day at the circus.

I do feel that prickling sense of overstimulation fear return when Zierhut talks about the interim stuff, however:

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

"And then one nuance on that is: We do plan on making content that unlocks in between … you want to stagger out some content across those four months. It's not just patch day comes [around], here's a content fire hose, and now we're silent for four months. A lot of that is, hey, there's a time event calendar that gradually unlocks things and opens them up over those four months to give things a little bit more life instead of that all at once effect."

Still, given Forever's meant to be a horizontally-progressing game that doesn't have expansions (we'll need to see how that pans out), I might find these little tasks a lot more soothing than the looming feeling I have with WoW, where at any point it might suddenly become too late to get stuck into a season.

Ideally, these mid-patch trickles will be optional tasks I can get around to basically whenever, rather than something I feel pressured to get done just so I can stay up-to-date for whatever flashy system's trundling down the pipeline next. Hit me with that lo-fi update cadence, I'm ready for it.

#3984. Phantom Blade Zero is asking players to free up 300GB of space for pre-loading, double its actual 145GB file size

Pre-loads are live for Phantom Blade Zero, the debut action game from Chinese developer S-Game. Alongside news of the pre-load, the studio revealed the final set of PC requirements, including how much space the game is going to take up on your drive.

Once installed, Phantom Blade Zero will occupy a chonky 145GB of your precious storage space. However, to pre-load the game, you're going to need over double that - 300GB, seemingly for the decryption and decompression process. The developer explained in a Steam blog post that "temporary files and the complete game files must coexist during the unlock process". You'll get back the extra space once the game is installed, of course.

While a game requiring extra space for these operations is not uncommon, the fact Phantom Blade Zero's install size is already so large makes needing to free up double that ludicrous. Phantom Blade Zero also requires an SSD drive, and seeing as the global gen-AI-driven memory and storage shortages have made them unattainable to many, you're not likely to buy a new drive just to accommodate a single game.

High as they may be, those storage space requirements aren't likely to deter players from buying a copy. Indeed, the game is already predicted to be among the year's biggest hits, having already sold over 500,000 copies on Steam alone, according to some estimates.

Eurogamer reviewed Phantom Blade Zero. In her review, Emma Kent was critical of the game's underwhelming boss flights and its general lack of polish, which she said mar Phantom Blade Zero's otherwise fluid and cinematic kung fu-style action.

Phantom Blade Zero arrives 29th October on PC and PS5.
